User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm single, live in San Diego CA. My employer Desert Sun Logistics paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $8,900 doing graphic design for 3 clients, got $890 interest from Marcus savings account and $480 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,100/month, total space 850 sq ft. I paid $4,800 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $720 to Northwest Harvest (food bank) have the receipt, and had $780 in work supplies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Short answer up front
- Likely take the federal standard deduction ($13,850 for single, 2023) unless you have sizeable state & local taxes or other itemizable amounts you haven't listed. With the items you gave (only $720 charitable + maybe SALT), itemizing will almost certainly be less than the standard deduction.
- Your home-office deduction applies only to your self‑employment (graphic design) income (not your W‑2 job). You can use the simplified method ($5/sq ft = $825 for 165 sq ft) or the regular method (proportionate share of rent, utilities, etc., calculated on Form 8829). Because your rent is high, the regular method could give a much larger deduction and materially change your AGI (and whether you can claim student loan interest).
- Student loan interest (up to $2,500) is an above‑the‑line deduction but phases out for single filers with MAGI between $75k and $90k (2023). With the amounts you gave, you may be over the phaseout if you use the simplified home‑office method — but if you use the regular method (allocating a portion of your rent), your MAGI might drop below the phaseout and allow at least a partial deduction.
- Required federal tax forms: Form 1040; Schedule C (business profit/loss); Schedule SE (self‑employment tax); Schedule 1 (adjustments to income — e.g., half of SE tax); Form 8829 only if you use the regular home‑office method; Schedule A only if you choose to itemize. Schedule B only if interest + dividends > $1,500 (yours total $1,370 so not required).

Quick numbers (estimates) — two home‑office options
1) Simplified home‑office method (165 sq ft × $5 = $825)
- Business gross: $8,900
- Business expenses: supplies $780 + home office $825 = $1,605
- Net self‑employment profit ≈ $7,295
- Self‑employment tax ≈ $1,031 (you can deduct half ≈ $515 on Schedule 1)
- Total income before adjustments: wages $84,900 + net SE $7,295 + interest $890 + dividends $480 = $93,565
- AGI after half SE tax ≈ $93,050 → above the $90k student‑loan phaseout cap; likely NO student loan interest deduction.

2) Regular method (home office = 165/850 × annual rent $25,200 ≈ $4,889; you could also allocate a portion of utilities if you have them)
- Business expenses: supplies $780 + home office $4,889 = $5,669
- Net self‑employment profit ≈ $1,231
- Self‑employment tax ≈ $174 (half ≈ $87 deduction)
- Total income before adjustments: 84,900 + 1,231 + 890 + 480 = $87,501
- AGI after half SE tax ≈ $87,414 → inside the $75k–$90k phaseout range, so you could get a PARTIAL student loan interest deduction (rough estimate: a few hundred dollars of the $2,500). Exact allowed amount needs the precise MAGI calculation.

Which should you choose?
- If you use the regular method you get a much bigger home‑office deduction (and that can reduce or eliminate the student‑loan phaseout). The tradeoff: more recordkeeping and you must use Form 8829 and show exclusive/business use of that office area.
- The simplified method is easier and less documentation but likely gives a much smaller tax benefit in your case.

What’s deductible from what you listed
- Deductible regardless of itemizing vs standard:
  - Qualified business expenses (supplies $780) — on Schedule C
  - Home‑office deduction — on Schedule C (simplified or regular)
  - Self‑employment tax: you pay it (Schedule SE) and deduct half as an adjustment to income (Schedule 1)
  - Interest ($890) and dividends ($480) are reported as income (1099‑INT and 1099‑DIV). No extra deduction.
- Charitable gift $720 — deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). If you take the standard deduction, you do not get a federal deduction for that.
- Student loan interest $4,800 — up to $2,500 may be deductible (above‑the‑line) but fully or partially phased out if MAGI is in the $75k–$90k range for single filers. With the simplified home office you are likely over the phaseout; with the regular method you may be within the phaseout and get a partial deduction.
- Unreimbursed employee business expenses for your W‑2 job: NOT deductible (suspended under current law).

Forms / worksheets you’ll need (federal)
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (adjustments to income — half of SE tax, etc.)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business)
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — ONLY if using the regular method
- Schedule A (Itemized Deductions) — only if you decide to itemize
- Schedule B — only if interest + dividends > $1,500 (yours < $1,500)
- Keep 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC for freelance income, 1099‑INT (Marcus), 1099‑DIV (Fidelity), W‑2 from employer, receipts for charity and business expenses, rent payments and utility bills if using the regular home‑office method.

State (California)
- You’ll file CA Form 540. California generally follows federal rules for many items but has differences; SALT cap ($10k) is a federal limit — on your CA return you still report state taxes as required. Let me know CA withholding/property tax info if you want to estimate state tax.

What I recommend next
1. Decide if you’re willing to do the extra recordkeeping for the regular home‑office method (rent + utilities receipts). Given your high rent, it’s worth comparing both methods because the regular method likely gives a larger net tax benefit and may allow some or all of the student loan interest deduction.
2. Provide any missing numbers I asked for if you want a precise comparison:
   - Total state income tax paid or withheld for 2023 and any property tax paid
   - Any mortgage interest (if you own a home)
   - Any utilities amounts you’d like allocated to the home office (electric, internet, renter’s insurance)
   - Confirm whether your freelance clients issued 1099s and whether you had any other business expenses or retirement/HSA/IRA contributions
3. If you want, I can:
   - Run a precise comparison of simplified vs regular home‑office methods and show the exact federal taxable income / estimated tax owed, and whether the student loan interest deduction is allowed and how much
   - Draft an email to your tax preparer with these figures and a request to use the regular method (and list documents to attach)

Would you like me to run the side‑by‑side calculation for simplified vs regular home‑office (I can use the exact rent/utilities and any other expenses you provide)?
